 The Fed in Uncharted Territory with New Communication Policy
 Author: AGF Investments 
 November 6, 2026
 Print 
 After years of transparent communication, the US Federal Reserve (Fed) has adopted a more tight-lipped approach under new Chairman Kevin Warsh. The impact of this new style on the market has yet to be determined and might not be for a while.
 “It ultimately rests on credibility. If this Fed proves it can adopt appropriate policy, then the market will likely become comfortable with less information and communication,” says Tom Nakamura , Head of Fixed Income & Currencies at AGF Investments.
 “Between now and feeling comfortable with that notion is an unknown amount of time and volatility—both in the market and the economy—that we will have to deal with. It is going to be tough for the market to grasp onto what the Fed is doing and thinking.”
 This all began on June 15 th , 2026, when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held rates steady. The bigger story was an intentional shift in the communication of monetary policy through shorter statements and the omission of forward guidance.
 Warsh described the abbreviated statement at the time as being designed to “give you the facts” while saying that forward guidance—the practice of signaling future rate movements to markets—is “not well-suited to the current policy conjecture.”
 The Chairman also introduced five task forces designed to re-evaluate how monetary policy is implemented moving forward, focusing on communications, the balance sheet, the timeliness of information, productivity, and inflation.
 A phase-out of the colloquially known “dot plots” in the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) appears underway. Warsh declined to submit a dot and questioned their role in the broader reporting framework. The projections are of particular interest to investors seeking to gauge whether the Fed is leaning hawkish or dovish.
 This new style has, ironically, done little to dissuade predictors and prognosticators ahead of subsequent FOMC meetings, especially given how vocal other members of the Fed have remained in contrast to Warsh. The 25-basis point hike instituted on September 16 th came without much surprise even though it was the first increase in over three years. Markets effectively priced it in and looked through it without a hiccup.
 The next FOMC meeting on October 28 th was no different. The Fed’s decision to hold rates steady in advance of the U.S. Mid-term elections was expected even with the inflationary backdrop supporting another hike. The surprise was that the Fed announced it will reduce its number of rate-setting meetings from eight to seven in 2027, then just six in 2028.
 “It’s not necessarily good or bad; it’s just not something the market has really dealt with,” Nakamura adds. “A lot of central banks in the developed and emerging markets world have gravitated towards having eight meetings. We’ll see if this leads other banks towards reducing their number as well, but right now it feels like a bit of an experiment.”
 The real test could come if the Fed hikes in December. While a variety of factors foreshadowed their eventual decision in September, the choice of whether to raise rates again and—and if so, when—appears more complicated this time around.
 Historically, the FOMC has helped foster market stability through its statements by signaling future rate cuts or hikes. Skeptics fearing increased volatility as a byproduct of reduced guidance don’t appear to have been proven correct yet.
 The highly communicative style Warsh appears intent on reshaping rose to prominence following the 2008 financial crisis, when interest rates had effectively fallen to zero. The Fed used forward guidance to signal that rates would remain low for an extended period, helping to lower long-term interest rates and recalibrate investor expectations.
 This shift toward fundamentals appears designed to discourage pre-commitment to future actions, giving the Fed more flexibility to respond as conditions evolve while avoiding constraints imposed by previous guidance.
 Investors now have little choice but to work with the information the Fed chooses to provide—and learn to live without the information it does not.
